Where HVAC calls come from

A furnace that won't start on the first cold night creates an urgent search: "furnace repair near me", usually on a phone, often after hours. Whoever shows up and answers first usually gets the job. Planned work (replacements, new installs, tune-ups) is researched over days, and trust matters more than speed. You want to win both.

1. Own the map results for the jobs you want

Your Google Business Profile is where urgent calls start. Set "HVAC contractor" (or your most specific category) as primary, add secondary categories for services you really do, like "Furnace repair service" or "Air conditioning repair service", and list your service towns. If you offer emergency service, say so and keep your hours accurate. Nothing loses a call faster than a listing that says "Closed".

2. Name every job, in plain words

Homeowners search the problem, not "HVAC". "Furnace not turning on", "heat pump installation", "AC not cooling", "boiler repair". If your website only says "heating and cooling services", you're invisible to those searches. List each service you do, with a sentence on each, and name the brands you work on if that's a selling point.

3. Catch the calls you can't answer

Many HVAC searches happen at night and on weekends. If no one answers, the homeowner calls the next company. Give them a second way to reach you: a short quote or service request form, and a text-back from your phone system, so you can call them first thing in the morning.

An Enoma page lists your services and towns, puts your number one tap away, and has a request form that sends after-hours leads straight to you. See your page in 30 seconds, built from your Google listing.

4. Turn repair calls into maintenance plans

A maintenance plan (an annual or twice-yearly tune-up with a member perk like priority scheduling) turns a one-time repair customer into a recurring one. It also fills your schedule in the shoulder seasons and gives you a natural reason to be the company they call when it's time to replace the system. Offer it on every service call.

5. Market before the season, not during it

When the first cold snap hits, you'll be too busy to market. Do it in the weeks before: text past customers about furnace tune-ups in early fall and AC checks in spring, update your Google profile with a seasonal post, and make sure your page reflects what you're booking now.

6. Collect reviews that mention the problem you solved

"Came out at 9pm when our heat went out" is the kind of review that wins the next emergency call. Ask every satisfied customer, the same day, with a direct link. Here's how to get more Google reviews, with a text you can copy.

What about paid leads?

Lead marketplaces and Local Services Ads can fill a slow week, but you pay for every lead and often compete for the same homeowner. Get the free channels working first, then add paid ads once you know what a booked call is worth. More on that in our guide to Angi alternatives for contractors.

Common questions

How to get more HVAC customers without buying leads: common questions

How do HVAC companies get more customers?

Mostly from Google: a complete Google Business Profile with the right categories and service towns, a website that names each service (furnace repair, AC repair, heat pumps), steady reviews, and a way to capture after-hours requests. Maintenance plans turn one-time repairs into repeat customers.

What's the best way to get HVAC leads without paying for them?

Show up in the map results for urgent searches like "furnace repair near me", list every service you offer in plain words, ask every satisfied customer for a Google review, and give after-hours visitors a request form so you can call them back first thing.

When should HVAC companies do their marketing?

Before each season, not during it. Text past customers about furnace tune-ups in early fall and AC checks in spring, and update your Google profile and website before the first cold snap or heat wave, when you'll be too busy to do it.

Are HVAC maintenance plans worth offering?

For most small HVAC companies, yes. They create recurring revenue, fill the schedule in slower months, and keep you top of mind when the customer needs a replacement system.
